# GaussianObject
## Overview
GaussianObject reconstructs 3D Gaussian Splatting representations from sparse or partial inputs by initializing Gaussians with a visual hull and fine-tuning a pre-trained ControlNet to repair degraded rendered images generated by adding noise to each Gaussian's attributes [S1, unofficial]. It outperforms previous NeRF-based sparse-view reconstruction methods [S1, unofficial].
## How it works
**Steps:**
1. Initialize 3D Gaussians with the visual hull derived from the input views [S1, unofficial].
2. Add noise to each Gaussian's attributes to generate degraded rendered images [S1, unofficial].
3. Fine-tune a pre-trained ControlNet to repair the degraded rendered images [S1, unofficial].
4. Update the Gaussian attributes using the repaired outputs from the ControlNet [S1, unofficial].
**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:** The method relies on the quality of the visual hull for initialization [S1, unofficial]. Severe occlusions may require robust diffusion priors to hallucinate plausible geometry [G]. Note that removing Gaussians with incorrect depth values and utilizing Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss are attributed to prior methods in the source text, not GaussianObject [S1, unofficial].
## Subtopics

### ControlNet
ControlNet introduces additional conditions to guide the generative process, such as canny edge, human pose, and depth, allowing for fine-grained control over image modifications [S2]. It sets itself apart from unconditional diffusion models by conditioning on explicit spatial or structural cues rather than text alone, and is chosen when precise geometric or pose alignment is required during generation [G].

## Operating characteristics
**Performance:** Outperforms previous NeRF-based sparse-view reconstruction methods [S1, unofficial].
## Background
GaussianObject was introduced to improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction from sparse inputs by combining geometric initialization with diffusion-based refinement [S1, unofficial]. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting and ControlNet, addressing limitations of NeRF-based methods in sparse-view settings [S1, unofficial].
